lead: The phase rule answers one practical question: how many properties of a system can you choose before the rest are decided for you? It counts phases, components and equilibrium equations and returns a single number F, the degrees of freedom. Duhem's theorem extends the same counting to a closed vessel of known overall composition: pick any two independent intensive variables and everything else follows. Flash-drum specification, crystalliser control and distillation column design all rest on this count, so a wrong F sends a whole flowsheet in the wrong direction.
prereq: You need the equal-chemical-potential equations from criteria for phase equilibrium and stability, which the count subtracts, and the difference between intensive and extensive properties.

sections.h3: Count the unknowns, count the equations

blocks.text: A phase is a part of the system with uniform properties; π counts such parts. A component is a chemically independent constituent; C is the smallest number of them needed to describe the composition of every phase. A degree of freedom is an intensive variable you may change on your own without a phase appearing or vanishing; F counts them.

Inside one phase the intensive variables are temperature T, pressure and the mole fractions. The C mole fractions sum to 1, so only C − 1 of them are free. Temperature and pressure are common to all phases at equilibrium, so across π phases the unknowns number 2 + π(C − 1).

The equations are the equilibrium conditions from 6.1. Each component has one chemical potential, and it must match in every phase. Matching C components across π phases gives C(π − 1) equalities. Nothing else is needed, because the mole-fraction sums were already used up in the unknown count.

blocks.where: F is the number of degrees of freedom, C the number of components, π the number of phases; the 2 stands for temperature and pressure.

blocks.text: Pure water with liquid and vapour present: C = 1, π = 2, so F = 1. You may pick the temperature, and the pressure then sits on the vapour-pressure curve. Try to set both and one phase disappears.

A reaction ties species together, so species are not components. Count species S, independent reactions R, and any extra constraint a, then C = S − R − a. Independent means no reaction in the set is a sum of multiples of the others.

items: Example: N₂, H₂ and NH₃ with NH₃ ⇌ ½N₂ + 3/2H₂. S = 3, R = 1, so C = 2. Two components means one independent mole fraction per phase; the extent follows from reaction equilibrium.
The extra constraint a covers things like electroneutrality in a salt solution, or a known fixed ratio of two species.

blocks.text: Most laboratory and plant equipment runs at a fixed pressure — a fume hood at 1 atm, an open beaker at 1 atm, or a reactor vented through a pressure-control valve set at 2 bar. Freezing the pressure removes one variable and gives the reduced rule.

blocks.where: F is degrees of freedom, C components, π phases; the rule applies when either temperature or pressure is held fixed.

blocks.text: Water boiling in an open pan at 1 atm: C = 1, π = 2, so F = 1 − 2 + 1 = 0. At that pressure the boiling temperature is fixed at 100 °C; you have no freedom left. Raise the pressure in a cooker and the fixed temperature rises with it.

In a closed system of known overall composition, fixing any two independent variables fixes every remaining intensive variable and the amounts of all phases. When F = 2 the two may both be intensive; when F = 1 at least one must be extensive (a phase amount or the total volume, say). That statement is Duhem's theorem, and it is stronger than the phase rule because it also pins down how much of each phase is present.

Why, in one line: the phase amounts add π − 1 unknowns (they sum to the total) and the component balances add C − 1 independent equations (the overall fractions sum to 1). Unknowns go up by π − 1 and equations by C − 1, so the count becomes (C − π + 2) + (π − 1) − (C − 1) = 2.

Take binary vapour-liquid equilibrium with overall mole fraction z₁ fixed. Unknowns are temperature, pressure, x₁, y₁ and the liquid fraction, five in all. Equations are the two fugacity equalities plus one material balance, three in all. Fix temperature and x₁ and nothing is free: pressure and y₁ are fixed by the two equilibrium equations, and the material balance then fixes the liquid fraction. With T fixed the phase rule leaves F = 1 for the two-phase binary, so pressure, x₁ and y₁ lie on a pair of curves, not a surface (see 6.3).

examples.question: Find the number of degrees of freedom for each case. (a) Pure water with liquid and vapour present. (b) Ethanol–water liquid and vapour at a fixed total pressure of 1 atm. (c) A gas of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ at 1 atm in which NH₃ ⇌ ½N₂ + 3/2H₂ can occur. State which variables are free in each case.
steps: (a) One species, one reaction-free system: C = 1. Two phases: π = 2. F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1. Only one variable is free; choosing T fixes the pressure on the vapour-pressure curve.

(b) Ethanol and water do not react: C = 2, two phases π = 2, so C − π + 2 = 2. The pressure is already fixed at 1 atm, which uses one degree of freedom, so F = 2 − 1 = 1. That one variable is temperature; fixing it fixes x₁ and y₁.
(c) Species present S = 3 (N₂, H₂, NH₃). Independent reactions R = 1, since NH₃ ⇌ ½N₂ + 3/2H₂ relates all three. No other constraint, so C = 3 − 1 = 2.

One gas phase, π = 1. F = 2 − 1 + 2 = 3: temperature, pressure and one composition variable; once temperature, pressure and that composition variable are set, reaction equilibrium plus the sum of the mole fractions fixes all three species mole fractions.
At the stated 1 atm, pressure is used up: F = 3 − 1 = 2, namely temperature and one composition variable.
examples.answer: F = 1 for (a), F = 1 for (b) at 1 atm, and F = 3 for (c) generally, falling to F = 2 at 1 atm.

C_a, P_a = 1, 2
F_a = C_a - P_a + 2
C_b, P_b = 2, 2
F_b = C_b - P_b + 2 - 1
S, R = 3, 1
C_c = S - R
F_c = C_c - 1 + 2
F_c_fixed = F_c - 1
print(F_a)
print(F_b)
print(F_c)
print(F_c_fixed)

traps: Counting species as components when a reaction exists. Three species with one independent reaction give C = 2, not 3.
Adding the full +2 when the pressure is already fixed. Once the pressure is set, use F = C − π + 1, otherwise every answer is one too high.
Remembering that F counts intensive variables only. Phase amounts are extensive and are not degrees of freedom; Duhem's theorem is what brings them in.
Missing extra constraints such as electroneutrality in an electrolyte solution, which reduce C by one more.
Thinking any two intensive variables will do for Duhem's theorem. They must be independent; fixing T and the boiling pressure of a pure liquid is a contradiction, not a specification.

quiz.q: Define phase, component and degree of freedom in one line each.
quiz.a: Phase: a part of the system with uniform properties. Component: a chemically independent constituent, the smallest number needed to describe the composition of every phase. Degree of freedom: an intensive variable that can be changed independently without a phase appearing or disappearing.

quiz.q: State Duhem's theorem for a closed system.
quiz.a: In a closed system of known overall composition, fixing any two independent intensive variables fixes all remaining intensive variables and the amounts of all phases.

quiz.q: Why does the chemical-potential equality give C(π − 1) equations and not Cπ?
quiz.a: For each component, the first phase sets the reference chemical potential, and each of the other π − 1 phases must match it. That is π − 1 equalities per component and C(π − 1) in total; matching a phase with itself would give a trivial identity.

quiz.q: Ice, liquid water and water vapour are all present in a closed container. Find C, π and F, and say what the answer means physically.
quiz.a: C = 1 (only H₂O), π = 3, so F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0. No variable is free: the triple point has one fixed temperature and one fixed pressure for a pure substance.

quiz.q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), all three species are present. Find C and F.
quiz.a: S = 3 species, R = 1 independent reaction, no other constraint, so C = 3 − 1 = 2. π = 3 phases (two solids and one gas). F = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1: choosing the temperature fixes the CO₂ pressure.

quiz.q: A student fixes temperature and pressure for an ethanol–water mixture that has both liquid and vapour, and then claims x₁ and y₁ can still be varied freely. Explain the error.
quiz.a: For C = 2 and π = 2 the phase rule gives F = 2. Fixing temperature and pressure uses both degrees of freedom, so x₁ and y₁ are determined by the two fugacity equalities. The student has double-counted the freedom.

quiz.q: A sealed flask of known overall composition holds a binary liquid in equilibrium with its vapour. How many intensive variables must be fixed, and what happens to the phase amounts when you change one of them?
quiz.a: Duhem's theorem gives two. Fixing, say, T and the liquid mole fraction x₁ determines the pressure, y₁ and the liquid fraction. Change T alone and the liquid fraction shifts as material moves between phases, so the amounts change even though the overall composition is fixed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators run a degree-of-freedom analysis before they will solve a flowsheet: they count equipment variables, streams and specifications and refuse to converge if the count is wrong. The same rule classifies phase diagrams in metallurgy and ceramics, where C is read as the number of independent oxide components. Electrolyte and membrane systems add electroneutrality as the extra constraint a. Search next for degrees-of-freedom analysis in flowsheeting, and for the Gibbs phase rule applied to ternary alloy diagrams.
